idiom_name: abstract class with protected provided operations and a protected abstract sandbox method
implementation_notes: Java's abstract class with protected members is the chapter's structure verbatim: the base declares a protected abstract sandbox method and protected (normally non-virtual in intent) provided operations. The JDK uses the shape in AbstractList, where subclasses such as ArrayList maintain the protected modCount field and may override the protected removeRange(int, int), while the list algorithms themselves stay in the base; the manual's abstract-methods chapter describes the mechanics. Java's protected is also package-visible, so a base class in a shared package hands its primitives to every class in that package unless the base and its family live in their own package (or the module does not export it). Since Java 17 a sealed base with permits can additionally freeze the family while keeping the shared primitives, and final keeps a primitive from being replaced. What replaces the classic structure where behaviours hold no state is a default-method interface (the interface-default-primitives variant) or a composed services object passed into the behaviour; the abstract class stays the reference form when the family shares instance state or the sibling set must be closed with sealed.
pitfalls: Protected members are visible to the whole package: a base placed next to unrelated classes leaks its primitives, and a subclass in the same package can bypass the vocabulary by calling the engine itself.

A protected primitive that is not final can be overridden by a subclass, changing the vocabulary for its entire subtree; mark the primitives final when they must stay fixed, and leave the sandbox method the only overridable member.
Calling the sandbox method from the base constructor dispatches before the subclass's field initialisers run, so the behaviour sees null fields.
Java has no abstract enforcement on the base's protected fields: a primitive can be documented as 'call only' while nothing stops a subclass from writing to it.

variants.name: Interface with default-method primitives over required accessors
variants.idiom_name: interface whose default methods are the provided operations (Iterable.forEach / Map default-method shape)
variants.implementation_notes: Since Java 8 an interface method may have a body, so the provided operations can live on an interface: each default method implements one primitive in terms of a couple of required abstract accessors, and any implementor - including types that already extend another class - inherits the vocabulary. Iterable.forEach and the Map default methods (computeIfAbsent, merge, getOrDefault) are provided operations in exactly this sense, and the mechanism exists so an API author can add operations without breaking implementors. What it cannot do is hold state or prevent replacement: a default method is never final, so an implementor may restate a primitive, and a class implementing two interfaces whose defaults clash must override the member. Keep state-bearing sandboxes on an abstract class and use the interface form for stateless behaviour families.
pitfalls: A default method cannot be final, so any implementor may replace a primitive or the behaviour itself; the invariant lives in the interface's documentation, not in the contract.
Interfaces hold no instance state, so a primitive that needs shared fields must reach them through required accessors or the family must move to an abstract class.
A class that implements two sandbox interfaces with colliding default members must override the member explicitly, which is easy to miss until the compiler reports the diamond.
